name: Project manager
summary: Project manager interviews usually focus on how you plan work, handle risk and keep people aligned when things change. Candidates commonly report behavioural questions about delays, scope changes and difficult stakeholders, alongside questions on methods such as Agile, Scrum and Waterfall. For IT projects, expect some questions on the software development life cycle; certifications such as PMP or a Scrum certification may come up.
rounds: Hiring manager interview on past projects: their size, your role and the results
Scenario or behavioural round: delays, scope changes, conflicts and risks
Methods discussion: Agile, Scrum, Waterfall, estimation and tracking tools
Panel or stakeholder round with team leads (for some roles)
looks_for: Clear planning: scope, milestones, dependencies and owners
Spotting risks early and acting on them
Sharing bad news early and honestly
Handling scope changes without losing control of time and cost
Getting people across teams to agree and commit
Knowing when to use Agile, Waterfall or a mix

questions.text: Tell me about a project that was running late. What did you do?
covers: How you spotted it, and how far behind it was
The options you weighed: scope, people, deadline
What you told stakeholders, and how it ended

questions.text: Describe a time two stakeholders wanted conflicting things from your project.
covers: Each side's goal, and why it mattered to them
How you got them to agree, or escalated with clear options
The decision, and how you kept both sides on board

questions.text: Tell me about a project that missed its goals. What would you do differently?
covers: What happened, owned honestly
The warning signs you missed
What you do differently in projects now

questions.text: Tell me about a time someone on your team wasn't delivering. How did you handle it?
covers: What wasn't working, and how you found out
The conversation you had and the support you offered
The outcome for the person and for the project

questions.text: Tell me about a risk you spotted early that turned out to matter.
covers: How you identified it
What you did to reduce it, and who you told
What would have happened otherwise

questions.text: Walk me through how you'd plan a new project from kick-off to the first milestone.
covers: Goals, scope and stakeholders agreed in writing
Breaking the work down, estimating it and finding dependencies
A schedule, a risk list, and how you'll report progress

questions.text: When would you use Agile and when Waterfall? Give an example of each.
covers: Agile for changing requirements and frequent feedback
Waterfall for fixed scope, regulated work, or projects with heavy hardware or construction parts
Hybrid approaches you've seen work

questions.text: What does a Scrum Master do in each of the Scrum events?
covers: Sprint planning, the daily scrum, the sprint review and the retrospective, and what each is for
Removing blockers and protecting the team's focus
Coaching the team rather than directing it

questions.text: Halfway through a project, the client asks for a major new feature without moving the deadline. How do you respond?
covers: Understanding why they want it and what it's worth
Showing the impact on time, cost and quality
Options such as swapping scope or adding a phase, agreed through change control and in writing

questions.text: How do you estimate effort for work your team hasn't done before?
covers: Breaking it into smaller pieces and estimating with the people who'll do the work
Ranges, comparisons with past work, and story points where the team uses them
A buffer for unknowns, and re-estimating as you learn

questions.text: How do you track whether a project is on schedule and within budget?
covers: Milestones, burn-down or burn-up charts, and planned versus actual
Earned value in plain words, for larger projects
Status reports that flag problems early

questions.text: Explain the critical path and why it matters.
covers: The longest chain of dependent tasks, which sets the end date
Why a delay on it delays the whole project
Ways to shorten it, and their cost

questions.text: A key team member resigns two months before launch. What do you do?
covers: Handover and knowledge transfer while they're still there
Re-planning: sharing out work, bringing in help, adjusting scope
Telling stakeholders about the risk early

questions.text: How do you run a status meeting that doesn't waste people's time?
covers: A clear agenda focused on blockers and decisions
Routine updates shared in writing beforehand
Ending with owners and dates for each action

questions.text: How would you run a project with a team spread across several time zones?
covers: Overlap hours for key meetings and written updates for everything else
Clear ownership and decisions recorded where everyone can find them
Sharing inconvenient meeting times fairly

questions.text: Why project management? What do you enjoy about it?
covers: What you enjoy: bringing order, delivering, working with people
An example of a project you enjoyed running
The kind of projects you want to run next

questions.text: Which tools and certifications have helped you most, and what are you learning now?
covers: Tools you use day to day, such as Jira or a planning tool, and what for
Certifications you hold and what you actually use from them
What you're learning next

tips: Prepare stories with numbers: team size, budget or duration, how late things were, and what you recovered.
Show that you raise bad news early; interviewers listen for whether you hid problems or surfaced them.
Know the Scrum events and roles well, even for roles that aren't purely Agile; questions on them are common.
Separate your own decisions from the team's; answers that only say 'we' can hide what you did.
If you're moving into project management from another role, use projects you coordinated informally as evidence.
